chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 1 — A Room of State in King Lear’s Palace
paragraphs: Enter Kent, Gloucester and Edmund.
KENT. I thought the King favored the Duke of Albany more than Cornwall.

GLOUCESTER. So it always seemed to us. But now, in dividing the kingdom, it isn't clear which of the Dukes he values most—the portions are weighed so evenly that no scrutiny could choose between them.
KENT. Isn't this your son, my lord?
GLOUCESTER. His upbringing has been my expense, sir. I've blushed so often to acknowledge him that now I've grown shameless about it.
KENT. I don't follow you.
GLOUCESTER. Well, sir, this young fellow's mother did follow me—and grew round in the belly for it. She had a son in her cradle, sir, before she had a husband in her bed. Do you smell a fault?
KENT. I can't wish the fault undone, when the result is so fine a young man.

GLOUCESTER. But I have a son by law, sir, about a year older than this one—who is no dearer to me, though. Even if this rascal came into the world a little impudently, before he was sent for, his mother was beautiful, there was good sport in his making, and the bastard must be acknowledged. Do you know this noble gentleman, Edmund?
EDMUND. No, my lord.
GLOUCESTER. My Lord of Kent. Remember him from now on as my honored friend.
EDMUND. I'm at your lordship's service.
KENT. I must come to love you, and I'll work to know you better.
EDMUND. Sir, I'll strive to deserve it.
GLOUCESTER. He's been abroad nine years, and he'll go away again. The King is coming.
[Trumpet flourish within.]
Enter Lear, Cornwall, Albany, Goneril, Regan, Cordelia and Attendants.
LEAR. Attend the lords of France and Burgundy, Gloucester.
GLOUCESTER. I will, my lord.
[Exeunt Gloucester and Edmund.]

LEAR. Meanwhile we'll reveal our deeper purpose. Give me the map there. Know that we have divided our kingdom into three parts—and it's our firm intention to shake off all cares and business from our old age, conferring them on younger shoulders, while we crawl unburdened toward death. Our son of Cornwall, and you, our no less loving son of Albany—we have at this hour a settled will to publish our daughters' separate dowries, so that future strife may be prevented now. The princes, France and Burgundy, great rivals in our youngest daughter's love, have long been making their courting visit at our court, and are now to be answered. Tell me, my daughters—since we are now divesting ourselves both of rule, interest in territory, and cares of state—which of you shall we say loves us most? So that we may extend our largest bounty where nature is matched by merit. Goneril, our eldest born, speak first.

GONERIL. Sir, I love you more than words can express—dearer than eyesight, space, and liberty; beyond what can be valued, however rich or rare; no less than life itself, with grace, health, beauty, honor; as much as any child ever loved, or any father was loved; a love that makes the breath grow faint and speech fail. Beyond all measure of such things, I love you.
CORDELIA.
[Aside.] What shall Cordelia say? Love, and be silent.

LEAR. Of all these lands, from this line to that one, with their shadowy forests and rich plains, with plentiful rivers and wide meadows, we make you lady. Let this be perpetual for you and Albany's heirs. What does our second daughter say, our dearest Regan, wife of Cornwall? Speak.

REGAN. Sir, I'm made of the same metal as my sister, and rate myself at her worth. In my true heart, I find she names my very deed of love—only she falls short, since I declare myself an enemy to all other joys that the most refined senses can possess, and find that I'm happy only in your dear highness's love.
CORDELIA.
[Aside.] Then poor Cordelia—
and yet not so; since I'm certain my love weighs more than my tongue can speak.

LEAR. To you and your heirs let this generous third of our fair kingdom remain forever—no less in size, validity, and pleasure than what we gave Goneril. Now, our joy—although the last and least, for whose young love the vines of France and milk of Burgundy compete to be chosen—what can you say to win a third more lavish than your sisters'? Speak.
CORDELIA. Nothing, my lord.
LEAR. Nothing?
CORDELIA. Nothing.
LEAR. Nothing will come of nothing. Speak again.
CORDELIA. Unhappy as I am, I cannot heave my heart into my mouth. I love your majesty according to my bond—no more, no less.
LEAR. How now, Cordelia? Mend your speech a little, or you may mar your fortunes.

CORDELIA. My good lord, you have begotten me, raised me, loved me. I return those duties back as is right and proper—obey you, love you, and most honor you. Why do my sisters have husbands if they say they love you completely? When I marry, the lord whose hand takes my pledge shall carry half my love with him, half my care and duty. Surely I'll never marry like my sisters, to love my father all.
LEAR. But do you mean what you say?
CORDELIA. Yes, my good lord.
LEAR. So young, and so unfeeling?
CORDELIA. So young, my lord, and true.

LEAR. Let it be so, then. Your truth shall be your dowry. By the sacred light of the sun, by the mysteries of Hecate and the night, by all the workings of the heavenly bodies, from which we exist and cease to be—here I disclaim all my fatherly care, all kinship and blood-tie with you. From now on I hold you a stranger to my heart and to me. The barbarous Scythian, or the cannibal who feeds on his own children to glut his appetite, shall find as much love, pity, and relief at my bosom as you, my former daughter.
KENT. My good liege—

LEAR. Quiet, Kent! Come not between the dragon and his wrath. I loved her most, and meant to rest my last days on her tender care. [To Cordelia.] Get out, and avoid my sight! May my grave be my only peace, since I now tear her father's heart from her. Call France. Who's stirring? Call Burgundy! Cornwall and Albany, take this third along with my two other daughters' dowries. Let her pride—what she calls plainness—marry her. I invest you both jointly with my power, pre-eminence, and all the large effects that accompany majesty. We ourself, by monthly turns, with a reserved retinue of a hundred knights to be maintained by you, shall make our abode with each of you in turn. Only we will keep the name and all the addition of a king. The rule, revenue, and execution of the rest, beloved sons, are yours. And to confirm this, divide this coronet between you.
[Giving the crown.]
KENT. Royal Lear—whom I have always honored as my king, loved as my father, followed as my master, remembered in my prayers as my great patron—
LEAR. The bow is bent and drawn. Get out of the arrow's path.

KENT. Let it fall, then, even if the forked head pierces my heart. Let Kent be ill-mannered when Lear is mad. What are you doing, old man? Do you think duty will be afraid to speak, when power bows to flattery? Honor is bound to plainness when majesty falls into folly. Reverse your decision—and in your best judgment check this hideous rashness. I'll stake my life on this verdict: your youngest daughter does not love you least. Those whose voices are low are not necessarily empty-hearted.
LEAR. Kent, on your life, no more.
KENT. I have always held my life as nothing more than a pawn to wager against your enemies. I'll never fear to lose it, when your safety is at stake.
LEAR. Out of my sight!
KENT. See better, Lear—and let me still remain the true target of your eye.
LEAR. Now, by Apollo—
KENT. Now by Apollo, King, you swear by your gods in vain.
LEAR. Oh, vassal! Heretic!
[Laying his hand on his sword.]
ALBANY and CORNWALL. Dear sir, hold back!
KENT. Kill your physician, and pay the fee to the foul disease. Take back your gift, or while I can still cry out from my throat, I'll tell you that you are doing evil.

LEAR. Hear me, traitor! On your loyalty, hear me! Since you have tried to make us break our vows—which we have never dared do before—and with strained pride to come between our sentences and our power, which neither our nature nor our position can endure, our potency being absolute, take your reward. Five days we allow you for provisions, to shield you from the world's disasters. On the sixth day you'll turn your hated back upon our kingdom. If, on the next day following, your banished body is found within our lands, that moment is your death. Away! By Jupiter, this will not be revoked.
KENT. Farewell, King. Since you'll show yourself this way, freedom lives elsewhere, and banishment is here.
[To Cordelia.] May the gods take you to their dear shelter, maid,
you who think justly and have spoken most rightly!
[To Goneril and Regan.] And may your large speeches be matched by your deeds,
so that good results may spring from words of love. Thus Kent, O princes, bids you all farewell. He'll shape his old course in a new country.
[Exit.]
Flourish. Re-enter Gloucester, with France, Burgundy and Attendants.
CORDELIA. Here's France and Burgundy, my noble lord.
LEAR. My Lord of Burgundy, we address you first, since you have competed with this king for our daughter. What's the least dowry you'll require with her, or will you give up your courtship?
BURGUNDY. Most royal majesty, I ask no more than your highness has offered, and I don't suppose you'll offer less.

LEAR. Right noble Burgundy—when she was dear to us, we held her dear. But now her price has fallen. Sir, there she stands. If anything in that small substance, or all of it, with our displeasure added in and nothing more, fits your grace's liking, she's there, and she's yours.
BURGUNDY. I don't know what to say.
LEAR. Will you—with all the faults she carries, friendless, newly adopted into our hatred, dowered only with our curse, and made a stranger by our oath—take her or leave her?
BURGUNDY. Pardon me, royal sir. A choice can't be made on such terms.

LEAR. Then leave her, sir. By the power that made me, I've told you all her wealth. [To France.] As for you, great king, I wouldn't draw your love so far astray as to match you where I hate. So I beg you to direct your liking some worthier way than toward a wretch whom nature is almost ashamed to call her own.

FRANCE. This is very strange—that she who only just now was your best object, the argument of your praise, the comfort of your old age, the best, the dearest, should in this brief moment commit something so monstrous as to strip away so many folds of favor. Surely her offense must be unnatural to a monstrous degree, or your earlier affection must be tainted. To believe such a thing of her would require a faith that reason without a miracle could never plant in me.

CORDELIA. I beg your majesty—if it's because I lack that smooth and oily art of speaking what I don't mean (since what I truly intend, I'll do before I speak)—make it known that it isn't a vicious flaw, murder, or filth, no unchaste action or dishonored step, that has lost me your grace and favor. It's only the lack of something I'm richer without: a constantly-soliciting eye, and such a tongue as I'm glad I don't have, though not having it has cost me your liking.
LEAR. You'd better not have been born than to have pleased me no better.

FRANCE. Is that all?—a slowness of nature that often leaves the action unspoken that it intends to do? My lord of Burgundy, what do you say to the lady? Love is not love when it's mingled with considerations that stand off from the central point. Will you have her? She herself is a dowry.
BURGUNDY. Royal King, give only the portion you yourself proposed, and here I take Cordelia by the hand, Duchess of Burgundy.
LEAR. Nothing. I have sworn. I am firm.
BURGUNDY. I'm sorry then, that you have lost a father in such a way that you must lose a husband too.
CORDELIA. Peace be with Burgundy! Since his love is based on regards of fortune, I shall not be his wife.

FRANCE. Fairest Cordelia—most rich in being poor, most chosen in being forsaken, most loved in being despised! You and your virtues I seize upon here. Let it be lawful: I take up what's cast away. Gods, gods! It's strange that from their coldest neglect my love should kindle into burning respect. Your dowerless daughter, King, thrown to my chance, is queen of us, of ours, and of our fair France. Not all the dukes of watery Burgundy can buy this priceless maid from me. Bid them farewell, Cordelia, though they're unkind. You lose here, but you'll find a better place there.
LEAR. You have her, France. Let her be yours. We have no such daughter, nor shall ever see that face of hers again. So be gone, without our grace, our love, or our blessing. Come, noble Burgundy.
[Flourish. Exeunt Lear, Burgundy, Cornwall, Albany, Gloucester and Attendants.]
FRANCE. Say farewell to your sisters.

CORDELIA. The jewels of our father—with washed eyes, Cordelia leaves you. I know you for what you are, and as a sister I'm most reluctant to call your faults by their proper names. Love our father well. To your professed bosoms I commit him. But yet, alas, if I still stood in his grace, I would prefer him to a better place. So farewell to you both.
REGAN. Don't prescribe our duties to us.
GONERIL. Let your study be to please your lord, who has received you as fortune's charity case. You have skimped on obedience, and you well deserve the want you've come to.
CORDELIA. Time will unfold what cunning hides—when faults are covered, shame mocks them in the end. May you prosper well.
FRANCE. Come, my fair Cordelia.
[Exeunt France and Cordelia.]
GONERIL. Sister, I have no small amount to say about what concerns us both most nearly. I think our father will leave here tonight.
REGAN. That's most certain—and with you. Next month, with us.
GONERIL. You see how full of changes his old age is. We've observed it plenty already. He always loved our sister most—and the poor judgment with which he's just cast her off shows too crudely.
REGAN. It's the infirmity of his age. Yet he has only ever slenderly known himself.

GONERIL. The best and soundest period of his life has been rash. So now we must expect from his old age not only the imperfections of his long-ingrained character, but also the unruly waywardness that infirm and choleric years bring with them.
REGAN. We're likely to have such inconstant outbursts from him as this banishment of Kent.

GONERIL. There's still more leave-taking ceremony between France and him. Please, let us join forces. If our father carries authority with the temperament he's showing now, this surrender of his will only end up offending us.
REGAN. We'll think further about it.
GONERIL. We must do something, and while it's hot.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 2 — A Hall in the Earl of Gloucester’s Castle
paragraphs: Enter Edmund with a letter.

EDMUND. You, Nature, are my goddess. To your law my services are bound. Why should I stand under the plague of custom and let the prudery of nations rob me? Because I'm some twelve or fourteen months younger than a brother? Why bastard? Why base? When my body is as well-made, my mind as generous, and my shape as true as honest madam's offspring? Why do they brand us with base? With baseness? Bastardy? Base, base? We who, in the lusty stealth of nature, take more composition and fierce quality than is poured—within a dull, stale, tired bed—into the creating of a whole tribe of fops, got between asleep and wake? Well then, legitimate Edgar, I must have your lands. Our father's love is the same to bastard Edmund as to the legitimate. Fine word—legitimate! Well, my legitimate, if this letter does its work and my invention thrives, base Edmund shall top the legitimate. I grow, I prosper. Now, gods, stand up for bastards!
Enter Gloucester.

GLOUCESTER. Kent banished like this! And France gone off in anger! And the King gone tonight! His power prescribed, confined to an allowance! All this done on the spur of the moment!—Edmund, what's this? What news?
EDMUND. If it please your lordship, none.
[Putting up the letter.]
GLOUCESTER. Why do you so eagerly try to put that letter away?
EDMUND. I know of no news, my lord.
GLOUCESTER. What paper were you reading?
EDMUND. Nothing, my lord.

GLOUCESTER. No? Then why did you need to dispatch it so hastily into your pocket? The quality of nothing doesn't usually need to hide itself. Let's see. Come on—if it's nothing, I won't need spectacles.
EDMUND. I beg you, sir, pardon me. It's a letter from my brother that I haven't fully read—and from what I've gone through, I don't find it fit for your viewing.
GLOUCESTER. Give me the letter, sir.
EDMUND. I'll offend whether I keep it back or hand it over. The contents, as far as I understand them, are reprehensible.
GLOUCESTER. Let's see, let's see!
EDMUND. I hope, for my brother's vindication, he wrote it merely as a trial, a taste of my character.
GLOUCESTER.
[Reads.] 'This policy and reverence of age makes the world

bitter to the best years of our lives—keeps our fortunes from us until our old age can't enjoy them. I'm beginning to find this oppression of aged tyranny an idle and pointless bondage—it rules not because it has power, but because it's tolerated. Come to me, so we may speak more of this. If our father would sleep until I woke him, you would enjoy half his revenue forever, and live as the beloved of your brother, EDGAR.' Hmm! Conspiracy? 'Sleep till I wake him, you should enjoy half his revenue.' My son Edgar! Did he have a hand to write this? A heart and brain to breed it in? When did this come to you? Who brought it?
EDMUND. It wasn't brought to me, my lord—that's the cunning of it. I found it thrown in at the window of my room.
GLOUCESTER. You know the handwriting to be your brother's?
EDMUND. If the matter were good, my lord, I'd dare swear it was his. But considering what it contains, I'd much rather think it wasn't.
GLOUCESTER. It is his.
EDMUND. It's his handwriting, my lord—but I hope his heart isn't in the contents.
GLOUCESTER. Has he never sounded you out on this business before?
EDMUND. Never, my lord. But I have heard him often maintain that when sons reach maturity and fathers decline, the father should be a ward to the son, and the son should manage his revenue.

GLOUCESTER. Oh, villain, villain! His very opinion in the letter! Abhorred villain! Unnatural, detested, brutish villain! Worse than brutish! Go, sirrah, find him. I'll have him arrested. Abominable villain—where is he?

EDMUND. I don't know exactly, my lord. If it would please you to suspend your indignation against my brother until you can derive better evidence from him of his intent, you'd be on a sure course. But if you proceed violently against him while mistaking his purpose, it would make a great gap in your own honor and shake the heart of his obedience to pieces. I dare wager my life that he wrote this to test my affection toward your honor, and for no other dangerous purpose.
GLOUCESTER. You think so?
EDMUND. If your honor judges it fitting, I'll place you where you can hear us discuss this, and through your own hearing you'll have your satisfaction—and with no longer delay than this very evening.
GLOUCESTER. He can't be such a monster.
EDMUND. Surely he isn't.

GLOUCESTER. —to his father, who loves him so tenderly and entirely. Heaven and earth! Edmund, seek him out. Worm your way into his confidence, I beg you. Frame the business according to your own wisdom. I would give up my estate to be in a proper resolution.
EDMUND. I'll seek him out at once, sir. I'll arrange the business as I find the means, and inform you of it.

GLOUCESTER. These recent eclipses of the sun and moon mean no good to us. Though the wisdom of Nature can rationalize them this way and that, yet nature itself finds itself scourged by the consequent effects. Love cools, friendship falls off, brothers divide. In cities, mutinies; in countries, discord; in palaces, treason; and the bond between son and father cracked. This villain of mine fits the prediction—there's son against father. The King falls away from the natural bent—there's father against child. We've seen the best of our time. Machinations, hollowness, treachery, and all ruinous disorders will follow us uneasily to our graves. Find out this villain, Edmund—it will cost you nothing; do it carefully. And the noble and true-hearted Kent banished! His offense, honesty! It's strange.
[Exit.]

EDMUND. This is the excellent foolery of the world: that when we're sick in our fortunes—often the result of overindulgence in our own behavior—we make the sun, the moon, and the stars guilty of our disasters. As if we were villains by necessity, fools by heavenly compulsion, knaves, thieves, and traitors by celestial influence, drunkards, liars, and adulterers by an enforced obedience to planetary force, and all that we are evil in by a divine shove. An admirable dodge of whoremaster man, to charge his goatish disposition to a star. My father coupled with my mother under the dragon's tail, and my birth was under Ursa Major—so it follows I am rough and lecherous. Bah! I'd be what I am if the most virginal star in the firmament had twinkled on my bastardizing.
Enter Edgar.
Right on cue! Here he comes, like the catastrophe in an old comedy. My cue is villainous melancholy, with a sigh like Tom o' Bedlam. Oh, these eclipses do foretell these divisions! Fa, sol, la, mi.
EDGAR. How now, brother Edmund, what serious thought has hold of you?
EDMUND. I'm thinking, brother, of a prediction I read the other day about what should follow these eclipses.
EDGAR. Do you busy yourself with that?

EDMUND. I promise you, the effects he writes about turn out unhappily: unnatural behavior between child and parent, death, famine, the dissolution of ancient friendships, divisions in the state, threats and curses against King and nobles, needless suspicions, banishment of friends, the scattering of armies, marital breakups, and I don't know what else.
EDGAR. How long have you been a follower of astrology?
EDMUND. Come, come! When did you see my father last?
EDGAR. Last night.
EDMUND. Did you speak with him?
EDGAR. Yes, for two hours straight.
EDMUND. Did you part on good terms? Did you notice any displeasure in him, in word or look?
EDGAR. None at all.

EDMUND. Think hard about how you may have offended him. And, at my entreaty, stay away from him until some little time has cooled the heat of his displeasure—which at this moment rages so in him that it would scarcely be quieted by harm to your person.
EDGAR. Some villain has slandered me.

EDMUND. That's my fear. Please, exercise restrained patience till the speed of his rage slows down. And as I say, withdraw to my lodgings with me, from where I'll suitably bring you to hear what my lord says. Please, go—here's my key. If you do go out, go armed.
EDGAR. Armed, brother?

EDMUND. Brother, I advise you for the best. I am no honest man if there's any good intent toward you. I've told you what I've seen and heard—but only faintly; nothing like the full image and horror of it. Please, go away!
EDGAR. Shall I hear from you soon?
EDMUND. I'll serve you in this business.
[Exit Edgar.]

A credulous father! And a brother so noble whose nature is so far from doing harms that he suspects none. On his foolish honesty my schemes ride easy! I see the way of it. Let me, if not by birth, have lands by wit. Whatever I can shape to fit, suits me.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 3 — A Room in the Duke of Albany’s Palace
paragraphs: Enter Goneril and Oswald.
GONERIL. Did my father strike my gentleman for scolding his fool?
OSWALD. Yes, madam.

GONERIL. By day and night, he wrongs me! Every hour he breaks out into some gross offense or another, setting us all at odds. I won't endure it. His knights are turning rowdy, and he himself reproaches us over every trifle. When he returns from hunting, I won't speak with him. Say I'm sick. If you fall short of your former services, that will be just fine. I'll answer for the fault.
[Horns within.]
OSWALD. He's coming, madam. I hear him.

GONERIL. Put on whatever weary neglect you please, you and your fellows. I want it to come to a confrontation. If he doesn't like it, let him go to our sister, whose mind and mine, I know, are one on this: not to be overruled. Idle old man, who still wants to manage the authorities he's given away! Now, by my life, old fools are babies again, and must be handled with rebukes as well as flatteries when they're seen abusing their position. Remember what I've said.
OSWALD. Very well, madam.

GONERIL. And let his knights get colder looks among you. What comes of it doesn't matter. Advise your fellows the same way. I want to breed occasions for confrontation here, and I will—so that I may speak out. I'll write at once to my sister to follow my very course. Prepare for dinner.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 4 — A Hall in Albany’s Palace
paragraphs: Enter Kent, disguised.

KENT. If I can borrow other accents as well as I've disguised my appearance, accents that will defuse my speech, my good intentions may carry through to that full result for which I disguised my likeness. Now, banished Kent—if you can serve where you stand condemned, it may come to pass that your master, whom you love, shall find you full of labors.
Horns within. Enter King Lear, Knights and Attendants.
LEAR. Don't let me wait one bit for dinner—go and get it ready.
[Exit an Attendant.]
Well, what's this? Who are you?
KENT. A man, sir.
LEAR. What do you do for a living? What do you want from us?

KENT. I profess to be no less than I seem—to serve truly any man who will trust me, to love the honest man, to converse with the wise man who says little, to fear judgment, to fight when I have no choice, and to eat no fish.
LEAR. Who are you?
KENT. A very honest-hearted fellow, and as poor as the King.
LEAR. If you are as poor for a subject as he's poor for a king, you're poor enough. What do you want?
KENT. Employment.
LEAR. Whom would you serve?
KENT. You.
LEAR. Do you know me, fellow?
KENT. No, sir. But you have something in your face I would gladly call master.
LEAR. What's that?
KENT. Authority.
LEAR. What services can you do?

KENT. I can keep honest counsel, ride, run, ruin a curious tale in the telling, and deliver a plain message bluntly. What ordinary men are fit for, I am qualified for, and the best of me is diligence.
LEAR. How old are you?
KENT. Not so young, sir, as to love a woman for her singing, nor so old as to dote on her for anything. I have forty-eight years on my back.
LEAR. Follow me—you shall serve me. If I like you no worse after dinner, I won't part with you yet. Dinner, ho, dinner! Where's my knave, my fool? Go and call my fool here.
[Exit an Attendant.]
Enter Oswald.
You, you, sirrah—where's my daughter?
OSWALD. If it please you—
[Exit.]
LEAR. What did that fellow there say? Call the blockhead back.
[Exit a Knight.]
Where's my fool? Ho, I think the world's asleep.
Re-enter Knight.
Well, where's that mongrel?
KNIGHT. He says, my lord, that your daughter is not well.
LEAR. Why didn't that slave come back to me when I called him?
KNIGHT. Sir, he answered me in the bluntest manner that he would not.
LEAR. He would not?

KNIGHT. My lord, I don't know what's going on, but in my judgment your highness is not being entertained with the ceremonious affection that you used to be. There's a great decline of kindness apparent in the general retainers as well as in the Duke himself and your daughter.
LEAR. Ha! Do you say so?
KNIGHT. I beg your pardon, my lord, if I'm mistaken—but my duty cannot remain silent when I think your highness wronged.

LEAR. You're only reminding me of what I've already suspected. I've noticed a very faint neglect lately, which I've preferred to blame on my own jealous over-sensitivity rather than on any real pretense or purpose of unkindness. I'll look into it further. But where's my fool? I haven't seen him for two days.
KNIGHT. Since my young lady's going to France, sir, the fool has pined away considerably.
LEAR. No more of that. I've noticed it well. Go and tell my daughter I want to speak with her.
[Exit Attendant.]
You go—call my fool here.
[Exit another Attendant.]
Re-enter Oswald.
Oh, you, sir—you, come here, sir. Who am I, sir?
OSWALD. My lady's father.
LEAR. 'My lady's father'! My lord's knave! You whoreson dog! You slave! You cur!
OSWALD. I am none of these, my lord. I beg your pardon.
LEAR. Do you trade looks with me, you rascal?
[Striking him.]
OSWALD. I will not be struck, my lord.
KENT. Nor tripped either, you base football player.
[Tripping up his heels.]
LEAR. I thank you, fellow. You serve me, and I'll love you.
KENT. Come on, sir, get up, away! I'll teach you the difference: away, away! If you want to measure your lout's length on the floor again, stick around—but away! Get going. Have you any sense? There.
[Pushes Oswald out.]
LEAR. Now, my friendly knave, I thank you. Here's a down payment for your service.
[Giving Kent money.]
Enter Fool.
FOOL. Let me hire him too. Here's my coxcomb.
[Giving Kent his cap.]
LEAR. Well, my pretty knave, how are you doing?
FOOL. Sirrah, you'd best take my coxcomb.
KENT. Why, fool?

FOOL. Why, for taking the part of one out of favor. No, if you can't smile as the wind sits, you'll catch cold shortly. There, take my coxcomb. Why, this fellow has banished two of his daughters and did the third a blessing against his will—if you follow him, you must necessarily wear my coxcomb. Well, nuncle! I wish I had two coxcombs and two daughters!
LEAR. Why, my boy?
FOOL. If I gave them all my living, I'd keep my coxcombs myself. There's mine—beg another from your daughters.
LEAR. Take heed, sirrah—the whip.
FOOL. Truth's a dog who must to kennel. He must be whipped out, while Lady Brach may stand by the fire and stink.
LEAR. A pestilent gall to me!
FOOL. Sirrah, I'll teach you a speech.
LEAR. Do.

FOOL. Mark it, nuncle: Have more than you show, Speak less than you know, Lend less than you owe, Ride more than you walk, Learn more than you trust, Wager less than you throw; Leave your drink and your whore, And keep behind the door, And you shall have more Than two tens to a score.
KENT. This is nothing, fool.
FOOL. Then it's like the breath of an unpaid lawyer—you gave me nothing for it. Can you make no use of nothing, nuncle?
LEAR. Why, no, boy—nothing can be made out of nothing.
FOOL.
[To Kent.] Please tell him—that's just what the rent of his land
comes to now. He won't believe a fool.
LEAR. A bitter fool.
FOOL. Do you know the difference, my boy, between a bitter fool and a sweet one?
LEAR. No, lad. Teach me.

FOOL. That lord who counseled you To give away your land, Come place him here by me— Or do you stand for him. The sweet and bitter fool Will presently appear: The one in motley here, The other found out there.
LEAR. Do you call me fool, boy?
FOOL. All your other titles you've given away. That one you were born with.
KENT. This is not altogether foolish, my lord.

FOOL. No, faith—lords and great men won't let me. If I had a monopoly on it, they'd want a share, and ladies too. They won't let me have all the foolishness to myself; they'll be snatching at it. Nuncle, give me an egg, and I'll give you two crowns.
LEAR. What two crowns shall they be?

FOOL. Why, after I've cut the egg in the middle and eaten up the contents, the two crowns of the eggshell. When you cleaved your crown in the middle and gave away both parts, you carried your ass on your back across the mud. There was little wit in your bald crown when you gave your golden one away. If I'm speaking like myself in this, let the man be whipped who first finds it so.
[Singing.]
Fools had never less grace in a year, For wise men have grown foppish, And don't know how to wear their wits— Their manners are so apish.
LEAR. When did you start being so full of songs, sirrah?
FOOL. I've been at it, nuncle, ever since you made your daughters your mothers. For when you gave them the rod and put down your own breeches,
[Singing.]

Then they for sudden joy did weep, And I for sorrow sung, That such a king should play peek-a-boo, And go among the fools. Please, nuncle, hire a schoolmaster who can teach your fool to lie. I would gladly learn to lie.
LEAR. If you lie, sirrah, we'll have you whipped.

FOOL. I wonder what kin you and your daughters are. They'll have me whipped for speaking true, you'll have me whipped for lying, and sometimes I'm whipped for holding my peace. I'd rather be any kind of thing than a fool—and yet I wouldn't be you, nuncle. You've pared your wit on both sides and left nothing in the middle. Here comes one of the parings.
Enter Goneril.
LEAR. Well now, daughter? Why that scowl on your forehead? It seems to me you've been frowning too much lately.

FOOL. You were a pretty fellow when you didn't need to care about her frowning. Now you're an O without a figure. I'm better than you are now. I am a fool—you are nothing. [To Goneril.] Yes, indeed, I'll hold my tongue. So your face bids me, though you say nothing. Mum, mum—He that keeps neither crust nor crumb, Weary of all, shall want some.
[Pointing to Lear.] That's a shelled peapod.

GONERIL. Not only this, sir, your all-licensed fool—but others of your insolent retinue are hourly carping and quarreling, breaking forth into gross and intolerable riots. Sir, I thought, by making this well known to you, to find a safe remedy. But now I'm growing fearful, from what you yourself have lately spoken and done, that you protect this conduct and encourage it by your indulgence. If you do, the fault will not escape censure, nor will the remedies sleep—which, in the interest of a healthy state, might in their working cause you the offense that would otherwise be shame, but which necessity will then call discreet proceeding.
FOOL. For you know, nuncle, The hedge-sparrow fed the cuckoo so long That it had its head bitten off by its young. So out went the candle, and we were left in the dark.
LEAR. Are you our daughter?
GONERIL. Come, sir, I wish you would make use of that good wisdom with which I know you are stocked—and put away these dispositions which lately transform you from what you really are.
FOOL. May not an ass know when the cart draws the horse? Whoop, Jug! I love you!

LEAR. Does anyone here know me? This isn't Lear. Does Lear walk this way? Speak this way? Where are his eyes? Either his perception weakens, his discernments are made lethargic. Ha! Am I waking? It can't be! Who is it that can tell me who I am?
FOOL. Lear's shadow.
LEAR. I would learn that—for by the marks of sovereignty, knowledge, and reason, I should be falsely persuaded I had daughters.
FOOL. Which they will make into an obedient father.
LEAR. Your name, fair gentlewoman?

GONERIL. This bewilderment, sir, is much in the style of your other recent pranks. I beg you to understand my purposes rightly. As you are old and reverend, you should be wise. Here you keep a hundred knights and squires—men so disordered, so debauched and bold, that this our court, infected with their manners, looks like a riotous inn. Gluttony and lust make it more like a tavern or a brothel than a gracious palace. The shame itself calls for immediate remedy. So be advised by her who will otherwise take by force what she asks for: reduce your retinue a little. And the remainder, who shall still depend on you, are to be such men as may befit your age, who know themselves, and you.
LEAR. Darkness and devils! Saddle my horses. Call my retinue together. Degenerate bastard! I won't trouble you. I still have one daughter left.
GONERIL. You strike my people, and your disordered rabble make servants of their betters.
Enter Albany.
LEAR. Woe to him that repents too late!—
[To Albany.] Oh, sir, have you come?
Is this your wish? Speak, sir.—Prepare my horses. Ingratitude, you marble-hearted fiend—more hideous when you show yourself in a child than the sea-monster!
ALBANY. Please, sir, be patient.
LEAR.
[To Goneril.] Detested kite, you lie.

My retinue are men of choice and rarest parts, who know all particulars of duty, and who in the most exact respect uphold the dignity of their name. Oh, smallest of faults, how ugly you appeared in Cordelia! Which, like an engine, wrenched my natural frame out of its fixed place, drew all love from my heart, and added to the bitterness. Oh, Lear, Lear, Lear!
[Striking his head.] Beat at this gate that let your folly in
and your dear judgment out! Go, go, my people.
ALBANY. My lord, I am guiltless—as I am ignorant of what has moved you.

LEAR. It may be so, my lord. Hear, nature, hear! Dear goddess, hear! Suspend your purpose, if you intended to make this creature fruitful! Into her womb convey sterility. Dry up in her the organs of increase, and from her degenerate body let there never spring a baby to honor her! If she must breed, create her child of bitterness, so that it may live to be a thwart, unnatural torment to her! Let it stamp wrinkles in her brow of youth, with falling tears wear channels in her cheeks, turn all her mother's pains and benefits to laughter and contempt—so that she may feel how sharper than a serpent's tooth it is to have a thankless child! Away, away!
[Exit.]
ALBANY. Now, gods that we adore, what is the cause of this?
GONERIL. Don't trouble yourself to know more of it. Let his disposition have whatever scope his dotage gives it.
Re-enter Lear.
LEAR. What, fifty of my followers at one stroke? Within a fortnight?
ALBANY. What's the matter, sir?

LEAR. I'll tell you. [To Goneril.] Life and death! I am ashamed that you have the power to shake my manhood this way, that these hot tears, which break from me involuntarily, should make you worth them. Blasts and fogs upon you! May the untended wounds of a father's curse pierce every sense in you! Old foolish eyes, weep over this cause again and I'll pluck you out and cast you with the waters you lose to temper clay. Ha! Let it be so. I have another daughter, who, I'm sure, is kind and comforting. When she hears this of you, with her nails she'll flay your wolfish face. You shall find that I'll resume the shape you think I've cast off forever.
[Exeunt Lear, Kent and Attendants.]
GONERIL. Did you mark that?
ALBANY. I cannot be so partial, Goneril, even given the great love I bear you—
GONERIL. Please, be content. What, Oswald, ho!
[To the Fool.] You, sir, more knave than fool—follow your master.

FOOL. Nuncle Lear, nuncle Lear, wait and take the fool with you. A fox when one has caught her, And such a daughter, Should sure to the slaughter, If my cap would buy a halter; So the fool follows after.
[Exit.]

GONERIL. This man has had good counsel.—A hundred knights! It's prudent and safe to let him keep a standing force of a hundred knights—yes, so that on every dream, every rumor, every whim, every complaint, every dislike, he may guard his dotage with their power and hold our lives at his mercy. Oswald, I say!
ALBANY. Well, you may fear too far.

GONERIL. Safer than to trust too far. Let me always remove the harms I fear, not always fear to be overtaken by them. I know his heart. What he has uttered I have written to my sister. If she supports him and his hundred knights, after I've shown her how unfit it is—
Re-enter Oswald.
Well now, Oswald! Have you written that letter to my sister?
OSWALD. Yes, madam.

GONERIL. Take some company with you and away on horseback. Inform her fully of my particular fears, and add to that whatever reasons of your own that may strengthen it. Get going, and hasten your return.
[Exit Oswald.]
No, no, my lord! This milky gentleness and conduct of yours—though I don't condemn it—still, pardon me, you are much more taken to task for lack of wisdom than praised for harmful mildness.
ALBANY. How far your eyes may pierce, I cannot say. Striving to better, often we mar what's well.
GONERIL. Oh, come now—
ALBANY. Well, well—we'll see how it turns out.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 5 — Court before the Duke of Albany’s Palace
paragraphs: Enter Lear, Kent and Fool.

LEAR. Go on ahead to Gloucester with these letters. Don't share anything you know with my daughter beyond what comes from her questions about the letter. If your diligence isn't swift, I'll be there before you.
KENT. I won't sleep, my lord, until I've delivered your letter.
[Exit.]
FOOL. If a man's brains were in his heels, wouldn't they be in danger of chilblains?
LEAR. Yes, boy.
FOOL. Then please, be merry. Your wit shall not go in worn-out slippers.
LEAR. Ha, ha, ha!
FOOL. You'll see your other daughter treat you kindly. Because though she's as like this one as a crab-apple is like an apple, still, I know what I know.
LEAR. What can you tell me, boy?
FOOL. She'll taste as much like this one as one crab-apple tastes like another. Can you tell why one's nose stands in the middle of one's face?
LEAR. No.
FOOL. Why, to keep one's eyes on either side of the nose—so that what a man can't smell out, he may peer into.
LEAR. I did her wrong.
FOOL. Can you tell how an oyster makes his shell?
LEAR. No.
FOOL. Nor I either. But I can tell why a snail has a house.
LEAR. Why?
FOOL. Why, to put his head in—not to give away to his daughters and leave his horns without a case.
LEAR. I will forget my nature. So kind a father! Are my horses ready?
FOOL. Your asses have gone to see to them. The reason why the seven stars are no more than seven is a pretty reason.
LEAR. Because they aren't eight?
FOOL. Yes indeed. You would make a good fool.
LEAR. To take it back by force!—Monster ingratitude!
FOOL. If you were my fool, nuncle, I'd have you beaten for being old before your time.
LEAR. How's that?
FOOL. You shouldn't have been old until you'd been wise.
LEAR. Oh, let me not be mad, not mad, sweet heaven! Keep me in my right mind. I would not be mad!
Enter Gentleman.
Well? Are the horses ready?
GENTLEMAN. Ready, my lord.
LEAR. Come, boy.
FOOL. She that's a maid now, and laughs at my departure, Shall not be a maid long, unless things be cut shorter.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 1 — A court within the Castle of the Earl of Gloucester
paragraphs: Enter Edmund and Curan, meeting.
EDMUND. God save you, Curan.
CURAN. And you, sir. I've been with your father, and given him notice that the Duke of Cornwall and Regan his Duchess will be here with him this night.
EDMUND. How come?
CURAN. I really don't know. Have you heard the news that's about—I mean the whispered ones, since they're still only ear-kissed rumors?
EDMUND. Not I. Tell me—what are they?
CURAN. Have you heard nothing of likely wars approaching between the two dukes, Cornwall and Albany?
EDMUND. Not a word.
CURAN. You will, then, in due time. Farewell, sir.
[Exit.]

EDMUND. The Duke be here tonight? The better! Best! This weaves itself into my schemes whether I will or no. My father has set a guard to seize my brother, and I have one delicate matter that I must act on. Brevity and fortune, work! Brother, a word—come down, brother, I say!
Enter Edgar.

My father is watching. Oh, sir, flee this place. Information has been given of where you're hiding. You now have the good advantage of night. Have you not spoken against the Duke of Cornwall? He's coming here, now, in the night, in haste—and Regan with him. Have you said nothing in his favor against the Duke of Albany? Think carefully.
EDGAR. I'm certain of it—not a word.

EDMUND. I hear my father coming.—Pardon me. As a stratagem, I must draw my sword on you. Draw. Seem to defend yourself. Now make a show of it. Yield—come before my father. Light there, ho! Flee, brother. Torches, torches!—So farewell.
[Exit Edgar.]
Some blood drawn on me will lend credit to my having fought more fiercely. [Wounds his arm.] I've seen drunkards do more than this in sport. Father, father! Stop, stop! No help?
Enter Gloucester and Servants with torches.
GLOUCESTER. Now, Edmund, where's the villain?
EDMUND. Here he stood in the dark, his sharp sword drawn, mumbling wicked charms, conjuring the moon to stand as his auspicious mistress.
GLOUCESTER. But where is he?
EDMUND. Look, sir, I bleed.
GLOUCESTER. Where is the villain, Edmund?
EDMUND. Fled this way, sir. When by no means he could—
GLOUCESTER. Pursue him, ho! Go after him.
[Exeunt Servants.]
—By no means could what?

EDMUND. Persuade me to the murder of your lordship. But when I told him the avenging gods bend all their thunder against parricides, and spoke of the many strong bonds binding a child to a father—sir, in short, seeing how loathingly I opposed his unnatural purpose, in fierce motion with his prepared sword, he lunged at my unguarded body and gashed my arm. But when he saw my best-roused spirits, bold in the quarrel's right, rallied to the encounter—or perhaps frightened by the noise I made—suddenly he fled.

GLOUCESTER. Let him fly far. Not in this land shall he remain uncaught, and once found—he's done for. The noble Duke my master, my worthy support and patron, comes tonight. By his authority I'll proclaim that whoever finds him shall deserve our thanks for bringing the murderous coward to the stake. He who conceals him—death.

EDMUND. When I tried to dissuade him from his purpose, and found him resolute to do it, with cursing speech I threatened to expose him. He replied, 'You propertyless bastard! Do you think if I stood against you that the weight of any trust, virtue, or worth in you would make your words be believed? No. What I should deny—as I would this—yes, though you produced my own handwriting, I'd turn it all back on your invention, plot, and damned scheming. You'd have to make a dullard of the world if they didn't think the profits of my death were very pregnant and potential spurs to make you seek it.'
GLOUCESTER. Oh, strange and hardened villain! Would he deny his letter, he said? I never fathered him.
[Trumpet within.]

Hark, the Duke's trumpets! I don't know why he comes. I'll bar all the ports. The villain shall not escape. The Duke must grant me that. Besides, his picture I'll send far and near, so that all the kingdom may have due notice of him. And of my land, loyal and natural boy, I'll work out the means to make you capable to inherit.
Enter Cornwall, Regan and Attendants.
CORNWALL. Well now, my noble friend! Since I came here—which I can call only just now—I have heard strange news.
REGAN. If it's true, all vengeance comes too short to pursue the offender. How are you, my lord?
GLOUCESTER. Oh madam, my old heart is cracked—it's cracked!
REGAN. What, did my father's godson seek your life? He whom my father named? Your Edgar?
GLOUCESTER. Oh, lady, lady, shame would have it hidden!
REGAN. Wasn't he companion with the riotous knights that attend on my father?
GLOUCESTER. I don't know, madam. It's too bad, too bad.
EDMUND. Yes, madam, he was of that company.

REGAN. No wonder then that he was ill-disposed. They are the ones who put him up to the old man's death, to have the spending and wasting of his revenues. This very evening I've been well informed of them by my sister, with such warnings that if they come to lodge at my house, I won't be there.
CORNWALL. Nor I, I assure you, Regan. Edmund, I hear that you have shown your father a child's proper duty.
EDMUND. It was my duty, sir.
GLOUCESTER. He revealed his scheme, and received this hurt you see, striving to apprehend him.
CORNWALL. Is he being pursued?
GLOUCESTER. Yes, my good lord.

CORNWALL. If he's caught, he shall never again be feared for doing harm. Frame the matter as you please, however you'll use my power. For you, Edmund, whose virtue and obedience so much commend themselves at this moment, you shall be ours. Natures of such deep trust we shall much need. You we seize upon first.
EDMUND. I shall serve you, sir, truly, in whatever capacity.
GLOUCESTER. For him I thank your grace.
CORNWALL. You don't know why we came to visit you?

REGAN. So out of season, threading our way through dark-eyed night. Occasions, noble Gloucester, of some weight, in which we must have the use of your advice. Our father has written, and so has our sister, of differences which I best thought it fit to answer from somewhere other than home. The various messengers from here await dispatch. Our good old friend, lay comforts to your bosom, and bestow your needful counsel on our business, which requires immediate attention.
GLOUCESTER. I serve you, madam. Your graces are right welcome.
[Exeunt. Flourish.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 2 — Before Gloucester’s Castle
paragraphs: [Enter KENT and OSWALD, from different sides.]
OSWALD. Good dawn to you, friend. Are you of this house?
KENT. Yes.
OSWALD. Where can we put our horses?
KENT. In the mud.
OSWALD. Please, if you care for me, tell me.
KENT. I don't care for you.
OSWALD. Well then, I don't care for you either.
KENT. If I had you locked up in Lipsbury pound, I would make you care for me.
OSWALD. Why are you treating me like this? I don't know you.
KENT. Fellow, I know you.
OSWALD. What do you take me for?

KENT. A knave, a rascal, an eater of leftover scraps; a base, proud, shallow, beggarly, three-suited, hundred-pound, filthy, worsted-stocking knave; a lily-livered, lawsuit-filing, son-of-a-whore, mirror-gazing, over-eager, finicky rogue; a slave who inherited nothing but a trunk; one who'd play the pimp out of a wish to please, and is nothing but a mixture of knave, beggar, coward, pander, and the son and heir of a mongrel bitch — one whom I will beat into howling tears if you deny a single syllable of what I've called you.
OSWALD. What kind of monstrous fellow are you, ranting at someone who neither knows you nor is known by you?

KENT. What a brazen-faced scoundrel you are, to deny you know me! Wasn't it just two days ago I tripped you up and beat you in front of the King? Draw your sword, you rogue: even though it's night, the moon is shining; I'll make a sop of moonshine out of you. Draw, you whoreson cullionly barber-monger, draw!
[He draws his sword.]
OSWALD. Get away! I have nothing to do with you.

KENT. Draw, you rascal — you've come with letters against the King, and you take Vanity the puppet's side against the royalty of her father. Draw, you rogue, or I'll slice up your shanks so badly — draw, you rascal, come on!
OSWALD. Help, ho! Murder! Help!
KENT. Strike, you slave — stand and fight, rogue, stand; you neat slave, strike!
[Beats him.]
OSWALD. Help, ho! Murder! Murder!
[Enter EDMUND, CORNWALL, REGAN, GLOUCESTER, and Servants.]
EDMUND. What's going on here? What's the matter? Stop!
KENT. With you, good boy, if you like. Come on, I'll bloody you; come on, young master.
GLOUCESTER. Weapons! Arms! What's the matter here?
CORNWALL. Keep the peace, on your lives — anyone who strikes again dies. What is the matter?
REGAN. They're the messengers from our sister and from the King.
CORNWALL. What's your quarrel? Speak.
OSWALD. I'm hardly able to catch my breath, my lord.
KENT. No wonder, given how hard you exerted your valour. You cowardly rascal, nature itself disowns you — a tailor made you.
CORNWALL. You're a strange fellow. A tailor make a man?
KENT. Yes, a tailor, sir. A stonecutter or a painter couldn't have made him so badly, even after only two years at the trade.
CORNWALL. Speak up — how did your quarrel start?
OSWALD. This old ruffian, sir, whose life I spared out of respect for his grey beard —

KENT. You whoreson Z! You unnecessary letter! My lord, if you'll give me leave, I'll grind this unbolted villain into mortar and use him to daub the walls of an outhouse. Spare my grey beard, you wagtail?
CORNWALL. Quiet, sir! You beastly knave, do you know no reverence?
KENT. Yes, sir, but anger has a privilege.
CORNWALL. Why are you angry?

KENT. That such a slave as this should wear a sword when he wears no honesty. Smiling rogues like this, like rats, often bite in two the holy bonds which are too intricately knotted to be untied; they smooth every passion that rebels in the nature of their lords; they bring oil to fire, snow to colder moods; they deny, they affirm, and turn their kingfisher beaks with every shift and turn of their masters, knowing nothing, like dogs, but following. A plague upon your epileptic face! Are you smiling at my speeches, as if I were a fool? Goose, if I had you on Sarum plain, I'd drive you cackling all the way home to Camelot.
CORNWALL. What — are you mad, old man?
GLOUCESTER. How did your quarrel start? Tell us.
KENT. No two opposites are more naturally hostile than I am to such a knave.
CORNWALL. Why do you call him a knave? What is his fault?
KENT. His face displeases me.
CORNWALL. Perhaps mine does too — or his, or hers.
KENT. Sir, it's my profession to be plain-spoken. I've seen better faces in my time than any sitting on any shoulder I see before me at this moment.

CORNWALL. This is one of those fellows who, having been praised for bluntness, puts on a brash roughness, and forces his manner completely out of his own nature. He can't flatter, not him — he's an honest, plain mind, he must speak the truth! If they accept it, fine; if not, he's plain. I know this sort of knave who, behind such plainness, harbours more craft and more corrupt ends than twenty silly-bowing courtiers who carry out their duties to perfection.
KENT. Sir, in good faith, in sincere truth, under the licence of your great appearance, whose influence, like the wreath of radiant fire on flickering Phoebus' face —
CORNWALL. What do you mean by this?

KENT. To speak out of the dialect you find so distasteful. I know, sir, that I'm no flatterer. He who deceived you in a plain accent was a plain knave, which, for my part, I will not be, even if I had to win your displeasure by begging you to make me one.
CORNWALL. What was the offence he gave you?

OSWALD. I never gave him any. It pleased the King his master quite recently to strike me, upon his misreading of the situation, when this one, in league with him and flattering his displeasure, tripped me from behind; once I was down, he insulted me, railed at me, and put on such a show of manliness that he earned praise from the King for attacking someone who had already given up. And now, in the swagger of that dreaded exploit, he's drawn on me here again.
KENT. None of these rogues and cowards but Ajax is their fool.
CORNWALL. Bring out the stocks! You stubborn old knave, you reverend braggart, we'll teach you.

KENT. Sir, I'm too old to learn. Don't call for your stocks for me — I serve the King, on whose business I was sent to you. You will be showing too little respect, too bold a malice against the grace and person of my master, by putting his messenger in the stocks.
CORNWALL. Bring out the stocks! As I have life and honour, he shall sit there till noon.
REGAN. Till noon! Till night, my lord — and all night too!
KENT. Why, madam, if I were your father's dog, you shouldn't use me this way.
REGAN. Sir, being his knave, I will.
[Stocks are brought out.]
CORNWALL. This is a fellow of the same kind our sister spoke of. Come, bring the stocks here!

GLOUCESTER. Let me beg your grace not to do this. His fault is great, and the good King his master will reprove him for it. The low punishment you intend is the kind reserved for the basest, most despised wretches for petty theft and ordinary trespasses. The King will take it badly that he, so slighted in the person of his messenger, should have him so restrained.
CORNWALL. I'll answer for that.
REGAN. My sister will take it even worse — to have her gentleman abused, assaulted, for following her business. Put his legs in.
[KENT is put in the stocks.]
CORNWALL. Come, my good lord, let's go.
[Exeunt all but GLOUCESTER and KENT.]
GLOUCESTER. I'm sorry for you, friend. It's the Duke's pleasure, and his disposition, as all the world knows well, will not be opposed or stopped. I'll plead for you.
KENT. Please don't, sir. I've stayed up and travelled hard. Some of the time I'll sleep through, the rest I'll whistle away. A good man's fortune may wear out at the heels. Good morning to you!
GLOUCESTER. The Duke is to blame in this — it'll be taken badly.
[Exit.]

KENT. Good King, you must confirm the old saying — out of heaven's blessing you've come into the burning sun. Approach, you beacon of this lower world, that by your comforting beams I may read this letter. Almost nothing sees miracles but misery. I know it's from Cordelia, who has most fortunately been informed of my disguised mission. And she will find time, away from this enormous state of affairs, to seek remedies for our losses. All weary and overwatched, take advantage of this, heavy eyes, not to behold this shameful lodging. Fortune, good night — smile once more, turn your wheel!
[He sleeps.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 3 — The open Country
paragraphs: [Enter EDGAR.]

EDGAR. I heard myself proclaimed an outlaw, and through the lucky hollow of a tree I escaped the hunt. No port is free, no place where guards and the most unusual vigilance aren't waiting to take me. While I can still escape, I'll preserve myself; and I've decided to take on the lowest, most wretched shape that poverty in its contempt of man ever brought near to a beast. I'll smear my face with filth, wrap a blanket round my loins, tangle all my hair into knots, and with naked exposure I'll face down the winds and the persecutions of the sky. This country gives me proof and precedent — the Bedlam beggars, who with roaring voices stick into their numbed and mortified bare arms pins, wooden splinters, nails, sprigs of rosemary; and with this horrible sight, from poor farms, paltry little villages, sheep-pens, and mills, sometimes with lunatic curses, sometimes with prayers, they force charity out of people. Poor Turlygod! Poor Tom — that's at least something. Edgar I am no longer.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 4 — Before Gloucester’s Castle; Kent in the stocks
paragraphs: [Enter LEAR, FOOL, and a Gentleman.]
LEAR. It's strange they should leave home like this, and not send back my messenger.
GENTLEMAN. From what I learned, the night before there was no intention on their part of this move.
KENT. Hail to you, noble master!
LEAR. Ha! Are you making this shame your pastime?
KENT. No, my lord.

FOOL. Ha, ha! He wears cruel garters. Horses are tied by the heads; dogs and bears by the neck; monkeys by the loins; and men by the legs. When a man is over-lusty with his legs, then he wears wooden leg-stockings.
LEAR. Who is it that so misunderstood your station as to set you here?
KENT. It's both he and she — your son and daughter.
LEAR. No.
KENT. Yes.
LEAR. No, I say.
KENT. I say, yes.
LEAR. No, no — they wouldn't.
KENT. Yes, they have.
LEAR. By Jupiter, I swear no.
KENT. By Juno, I swear yes.

LEAR. They wouldn't dare. They couldn't, wouldn't do it. It's worse than murder, to commit such violent outrage against the respect due to a king. Tell me, with all proper haste, how you could have deserved or they imposed this treatment, coming from us.

KENT. My lord, when at their home I delivered your highness' letters to them, before I had risen from the place where I kneeled in duty, there came a steaming messenger, soaked from his haste, half-breathless, panting out greetings from his mistress Goneril. He delivered letters, despite the interruption, which they read at once. On those contents, they summoned up their household, took horse straight away, and commanded me to follow and await the leisure of their answer. They gave me cold looks. And meeting here the other messenger, whose welcome I perceived had poisoned mine — being the very fellow who lately displayed such impudence against your highness — having more manliness than wisdom about me, I drew my sword. He roused the house with loud and cowardly cries. Your son and daughter found this trespass worth the shame it suffers here.

FOOL. Winter's not gone yet, if the wild geese fly that way. Fathers who wear rags make their children blind, but fathers who carry bags shall see their children kind. Fortune, that arrant whore, never turns the key to the poor. But for all this, you shall have as many sorrows for your daughters as you can count in a year.
LEAR. Oh, how this mother-fit swells up toward my heart! Hysterica passio, down, you climbing sorrow — your proper place is below! Where is this daughter?
KENT. With the earl, sir, here inside.
LEAR. Don't follow me. Stay here.
[Exit.]
GENTLEMAN. Did you give no greater offence than what you've told us?
KENT. None. How is it the King comes with such a small retinue?
FOOL. If you'd been set in the stocks for that question, you'd have well deserved it.
KENT. Why, fool?

FOOL. We'll send you to school to an ant, to teach you there's no labouring in the winter. All who follow their noses are led by their eyes, except blind men; and there's not a nose among twenty that can't smell out the man who's stinking. Let go your hold when a great wheel runs down a hill, lest it break your neck by dragging you with it; but the great one that goes upward, let him pull you after. When a wise man gives you better counsel, give me mine back: I'd have only knaves follow it, since a fool gives it. The man who serves and seeks for gain, and follows only for show, will pack his bags when it begins to rain, and leave you in the storm. But I will stay; the fool will remain, and let the wise man fly: the knave turns fool that runs away; the fool no knave, by God.
KENT. Where did you learn this, fool?
FOOL. Not in the stocks, fool.
[Enter LEAR and GLOUCESTER.]
LEAR. Refuse to speak with me? They are sick? They are weary? They have travelled all night? Mere excuses — the signs of revolt and breaking away. Get me a better answer.
GLOUCESTER. My dear lord, you know the fiery temperament of the Duke — how unyielding and fixed he is in his own course.
LEAR. Vengeance! Plague! Death! Confusion! Fiery? What temperament? Why, Gloucester, Gloucester, I want to speak with the Duke of Cornwall and his wife.
GLOUCESTER. Well, my good lord, I have informed them so.
LEAR. Informed them! Do you understand me, man?
GLOUCESTER. Yes, my good lord.

LEAR. The King wishes to speak with Cornwall; the dear father wishes to speak with his daughter — commands her, expects her service. Are they informed of this? My breath and blood! Fiery? The fiery Duke, tell the hot Duke that — no, but not yet: perhaps he is unwell. Infirmity always neglects all the duties our health is bound to: we are not ourselves when nature, being oppressed, commands the mind to suffer with the body. I'll hold back; and I'm out of patience with my own more headstrong will, for taking the indisposed and sickly fit for the sound man. [Looking on KENT.] Death upon my state! Why should he sit here? This act persuades me that this withdrawal of the Duke and her is calculated. Give me my servant back. Go tell the Duke and his wife I'd speak with them, now, immediately. Tell them to come out and hear me, or at their chamber door I'll beat the drum till it cries sleep to death.
GLOUCESTER. I wish everything were well between you.
[Exit.]
LEAR. Oh me, my heart, my rising heart! But down!

FOOL. Cry out to it, nuncle, as the cockney did to the eels when she put them in the pastry alive; she rapped them on the heads with a stick and cried 'Down, wantons, down!' It was her brother who, in pure kindness to his horse, buttered his hay.
[Enter CORNWALL, REGAN, GLOUCESTER, and Servants.]
LEAR. Good morning to you both.
CORNWALL. Hail to your grace!
[KENT is here set at liberty.]
REGAN. I am glad to see your highness.

LEAR. Regan, I think you are; I know what reason I have to think so. If you weren't glad, I'd divorce myself from your mother's tomb, since it would be entombing an adulteress. [To KENT.] Oh, are you free? Some other time for that. Beloved Regan, your sister's worthless. Oh Regan, she has tied sharp-toothed unkindness, like a vulture, here.
[Points to his heart.]
I can scarcely speak to you; you would not believe with what a depraved nature — Oh Regan!
REGAN. I beg you, sir, be patient. I have hope that you less know how to value her merit than she knows how to fall short of her duty.
LEAR. Say, how is that?

REGAN. I cannot believe my sister would in the slightest fail in her obligation. If, sir, perhaps she has restrained the riots of your followers, it's on such grounds, and to such wholesome end, as clears her from all blame.
LEAR. My curses on her.

REGAN. Oh, sir, you are old. Nature in you stands at the very edge of her confines. You should be ruled and led by some judgment that discerns your state better than you do yourself. Therefore I beg you, return to our sister; tell her you have wronged her, sir.
LEAR. Ask her forgiveness? Just observe how this becomes the household: 'Dear daughter, I confess that I am old;
[Kneeling.]
Age is unnecessary: on my knees I beg that you will grant me clothing, a bed, and food.'
REGAN. Good sir, no more! These are unsightly tricks. Return to my sister.
LEAR.
[Rising.] Never, Regan:

She has cut me down by half of my train; looked black upon me; struck me with her tongue, most serpent-like, upon the very heart. May all the stored vengeances of heaven fall on her ungrateful head! Strike her young bones, you blasting winds, with lameness!
CORNWALL. For shame, sir, for shame!
LEAR. You nimble lightnings, hurl your blinding flames into her scornful eyes! Infect her beauty, you fen-sucked fogs, drawn up by the powerful sun, so as to fall and blast her pride!
REGAN. Oh, the blessed gods! So you will wish on me when the rash mood is on you.

LEAR. No, Regan, you shall never have my curse. Your tender-hearted nature will not give you over to harshness. Her eyes are fierce; but yours give comfort, and don't burn. It's not in you to grudge my pleasures, to cut off my train, to bandy hasty words, to skimp my rations, and, in conclusion, to bolt the door against my coming in. You better know the offices of nature, the bond of childhood, the effects of courtesy, the dues of gratitude. You haven't forgotten the half of the kingdom in which I endowed you.
REGAN. Good sir, to the point.
LEAR. Who put my man in the stocks?
[Trumpet sounds within.]
CORNWALL. What trumpet is that?
REGAN. I know it, my sister's. This confirms her letter, that she would soon be here.
[Enter OSWALD.]
Has your lady come?
LEAR. This is a slave whose easy borrowed pride dwells in the fickle favour of her he follows. Out, varlet, from my sight!
CORNWALL. What does your grace mean?
LEAR. Who put my servant in the stocks? Regan, I have good hope you didn't know of it. Who comes here? Oh heavens!
[Enter GONERIL.]
If you love old men, if your sweet sway allows obedience, if you yourselves are old, make it your cause; send down, and take my part!
[To GONERIL.] Are you not ashamed to look upon this beard?
Oh Regan, will you take her by the hand?
GONERIL. Why not by the hand, sir? How have I offended? Not everything is offence that indiscretion finds, and dotage calls it so.
LEAR. Oh sides, you are too tough! Will you still hold? How came my man into the stocks?
CORNWALL. I set him there, sir; but his own disorders deserved much worse treatment than that.
LEAR. You? Did you?

REGAN. I beg you, father, being weak, seem so. If, till the end of your month, you will return and stay with my sister, dismissing half your train, then come to me. I am now away from home, and out of the supplies that would be needed for your proper entertainment.

LEAR. Return to her, and fifty men dismissed? No, rather I renounce all roofs and choose to wage war against the enmity of the air; to be a comrade with the wolf and owl — necessity's sharp pinch! Return with her? Why, the hot-blooded King of France, who took our youngest born without a dowry, I could as well be brought to kneel before his throne and, like a squire, beg for a pension to keep base life going. Return with her? Persuade me rather to be slave and pack-horse to this detested groom.
[Pointing to OSWALD.]
GONERIL. As you choose, sir.

LEAR. I beg you, daughter, do not make me mad. I won't trouble you, my child; farewell. We'll meet no more, see one another no more. But yet you are my flesh, my blood, my daughter — or rather a disease that's in my flesh, which I must call mine. You are a boil, a plague sore, an embossed carbuncle in my corrupted blood. But I'll not chide you; let shame come when it will, I do not call for it. I do not bid the thunder-bearer shoot, nor tell tales of you to high-judging Jove. Mend when you can; be better at your leisure: I can be patient; I can stay with Regan, I and my hundred knights.

REGAN. Not altogether so. I didn't look for you yet, nor am I provided for your fit welcome. Listen, sir, to my sister; for those who mingle reason with your passion must be content to think you old, and so — but she knows what she does.
LEAR. Is this well spoken?

REGAN. I dare to vouch for it, sir. What, fifty followers? Is it not well? Why should you need more? Yes, or so many, since both expense and danger argue against so great a number? How in one house should so many people, under two commands, hold harmony? It's hard; almost impossible.
GONERIL. Why couldn't you, my lord, receive attendance from those that she calls servants, or from mine?

REGAN. Why not, my lord? If then they happened to slack off with you, we could discipline them. If you will come to me — for now I spy a danger — I beg you to bring only five-and-twenty: to no more than that will I give place or take notice of.
LEAR. I gave you all —
REGAN. And in good time you gave it.
LEAR. Made you my guardians, my trustees; but kept the reservation of being followed by a set number. What, must I come to you with five-and-twenty, Regan, did you say so?
REGAN. And I say it again, my lord; no more with me.
LEAR. Those wicked creatures yet look well-favoured when others are more wicked; not being the worst earns some rank of praise.
[To GONERIL.] I'll go with you:
Your fifty yet is double five-and-twenty, and you are twice her love.
GONERIL. Hear me, my lord. What need have you of five-and-twenty? Ten? Or five? To follow you in a house where twice as many have a command to attend you?
REGAN. What need of one?

LEAR. Oh, do not reason the need. Our basest beggars are in the poorest thing superfluous. Allow not nature more than nature needs, and man's life is as cheap as a beast's. You are a lady; if to go warm were all that's gorgeous, why, nature wouldn't need what you wear gorgeously, which scarcely keeps you warm. But, for true need — you heavens, give me that patience, patience I need! You see me here, you gods, a poor old man, as full of grief as of age — wretched in both! If it is you that stirs these daughters' hearts against their father, do not so fool me as to bear it tamely. Touch me with noble anger, and let not women's weapons, water-drops, stain my man's cheeks! No, you unnatural hags, I will have such revenges on you both that all the world shall — I will do such things — what they are yet, I know not; but they shall be the terrors of the earth. You think I'll weep; no, I'll not weep: — [Storm and tempest.] I have full cause of weeping; but this heart shall break into a hundred thousand pieces before I'll weep. Oh fool, I shall go mad!
[Exeunt LEAR, GLOUCESTER, KENT, and FOOL.]
CORNWALL. Let us withdraw; there'll be a storm.
REGAN. This house is small: the old man and his people cannot be properly housed.
GONERIL. It's his own fault; he has driven himself from comfort and must necessarily taste his folly.
REGAN. For himself, I'll receive him gladly, but not one follower.
GONERIL. So am I resolved. Where is my lord of Gloucester?
[Enter GLOUCESTER.]
CORNWALL. Followed the old man out, but has returned.
GLOUCESTER. The King is in high rage.
CORNWALL. Where is he going?
GLOUCESTER. He calls for his horse, but to where I don't know.
CORNWALL. It's best to give him his way; he leads himself.
GONERIL. My lord, by no means beg him to stay.
GLOUCESTER. Alas, the night comes on, and the high winds blow sharply. For many miles around there's scarcely a bush.

REGAN. Oh, sir, to wilful men, the injuries that they themselves bring on must be their schoolmasters. Shut up your doors. He is attended by a desperate train, and what they may incite him to, being apt to have his ear abused, wisdom bids us fear.
CORNWALL. Shut up your doors, my lord; it's a wild night. My Regan counsels well; come in out of the storm.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 1 — A Heath
paragraphs: [A storm with thunder and lightning. Enter KENT and a Gentleman, from different sides.]
KENT. Who's there, besides foul weather?
GENTLEMAN. One whose mind is like the weather, most unquiet.
KENT. I know you. Where's the King?

GENTLEMAN. Struggling against the fretful elements. He commands the wind to blow the earth into the sea, or to swell the curled waters above the mainland, so that things might change or cease. He tears his white hair, which the impetuous blasts, with eyeless rage, catch in their fury and toss about as if it were nothing. In his little world of man, he strives to out-scorn the back-and-forth conflicting wind and rain. This night, when the cub-robbed bear would lie low, when the lion and the belly-pinched wolf keep their fur dry, he runs about bareheaded, and bids whatever will, take all.
KENT. But who is with him?
GENTLEMAN. None but the Fool, who labours to jest his heart-struck injuries away.

KENT. Sir, I do know you, and dare, on the warrant of my judgment, entrust a serious matter to you. There is division — though as yet the surface of it is covered with mutual cunning — between Albany and Cornwall. Both of them have, as those in high places do, servants who appear loyal but who are in fact spies and informers for France, intelligent about our affairs. There has been seen, either in the petty quarrels and intrigues of the Dukes, or in the harsh rein both of them have ridden against the old kind King, or in something deeper of which these may only be furnishings — but, true it is, from France there comes a force into this fragmented kingdom, which already, wise in our negligence, has secretly landed at some of our best ports and is on the point of unfurling its open banner. Now to you: if on my word you dare trust me so far as to make haste to Dover, you'll find some who will thank you for making a just report of how unnatural and maddening a sorrow the King has cause to lament. I am a gentleman of blood and breeding, and from some knowledge and certainty offer this task to you.
GENTLEMAN. I will talk further with you.

KENT. No, don't. For proof that I am much more than my outer appearance, open this purse and take what it contains. If you should see Cordelia — as fear not but you shall — show her this ring, and she will tell you who your companion is, whom as yet you do not know. Curse this storm! I will go and seek the King.
GENTLEMAN. Give me your hand. Have you no more to say?
KENT. Few words, but, to the point, more than all yet said: when we have found the King — and your task is that way, I'll take this way — whoever first comes upon him, let him hail the other.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 2 — Another part of the heath
paragraphs: [Storm continues. Enter LEAR and FOOL.]

LEAR. Blow, winds, and crack your cheeks! Rage! Blow! You cataracts and hurricanes, spout till you have drenched our steeples and drowned the weathercocks! You sulphurous and thought-swift fires, advance guards to oak-cleaving thunderbolts, singe my white head! And you, all-shaking thunder, strike flat the thick rotundity of the world! Crack nature's moulds, spill all seeds at once, that make ungrateful man!

FOOL. Oh nuncle, holy water at court, in a dry house, is better than this rainwater out of doors. Good nuncle, go in, and ask your daughters' blessing: here's a night that pities neither wise men nor fools.

LEAR. Rumble your bellyful! Spit, fire! Spout, rain! Neither rain, wind, thunder, nor fire are my daughters. I do not accuse you, elements, of unkindness. I never gave you a kingdom, called you my children — you owe me no allegiance. So let fall your horrible pleasure. Here I stand, your slave, a poor, infirm, weak, and despised old man. But yet I call you servile ministers, who will join with two pernicious daughters in your high-engendered battles against a head as old and white as this! Oh! Oh! It's foul!

FOOL. He that has a house to put his head in has a good headpiece. The codpiece that will house itself before the head has any, both the head and he shall have lice — so beggars marry many. The man that makes his toe what he should make of his heart shall, of a corn, cry woe, and turn his sleep to waking. For there was never yet a fair woman who didn't make faces at herself in a mirror.
LEAR. No, I will be the pattern of all patience; I will say nothing.
[Enter KENT.]
KENT. Who's there?
FOOL. Why, here's grace and a codpiece; that's a wise man and a fool.

KENT. Alas, sir, are you here? Things that love the night don't love such nights as these. The wrathful skies frighten the very wanderers of the dark, and make them keep to their caves. Since I became a man, I do not remember ever to have heard such sheets of fire, such bursts of horrid thunder, such groans of roaring wind and rain. Human nature cannot bear the affliction, nor the fear.

LEAR. Let the great gods, who keep this dreadful uproar over our heads, find out their enemies now. Tremble, you wretch, who has within you undivulged crimes unwhipped by justice. Hide yourself, you bloody hand; you perjurer, and you false imitator of virtue who are incestuous. Caitiff, shake to pieces, you who under cover and convenient seeming have plotted against a man's life. Close pent-up guilts, rive your concealing containers, and cry for grace from these dreadful summoners. I am a man more sinned against than sinning.

KENT. Alas, bareheaded! Gracious my lord, close by here is a hovel; it will lend you some shelter against the tempest. Rest there, while I go to this hard house — harder than the stones it's built of, which even just now, when I inquired after you, denied me entry — return, and force their stinted courtesy.

LEAR. My wits begin to turn. Come on, my boy. How are you, my boy? Are you cold? I'm cold myself. Where is this straw, my fellow? The art of our necessities is strange, that can make vile things precious. Come, lead on to your hovel. Poor fool and knave, I have one part in my heart that's sorry yet for you.
FOOL.
[Singing.]
He that has and a little tiny wit, with heigh-ho, the wind and the rain, must make content with his fortunes fit, though the rain it raineth every day.
LEAR. True, boy. Come, bring us to this hovel.
[Exeunt LEAR and KENT.]

FOOL. This is a brave night to cool a courtesan. I'll speak a prophecy before I go: when priests are more in word than in matter; when brewers spoil their malt with water; when nobles are their tailors' tutors; when no heretics are burned, but only the suitors of wenches; when every case in law is right; when no squire is in debt, nor any poor knight; when slanders do not live on tongues; nor cut-purses come into crowds; when usurers count their gold in the field; and bawds and whores build churches: then shall the realm of Albion come to great confusion. Then comes the time, whoever lives to see it, that going shall be done with feet. This prophecy Merlin shall make, for I live before his time.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 3 — A Room in Gloucester’s Castle
paragraphs: [Enter GLOUCESTER and EDMUND.]

GLOUCESTER. Alas, alas, Edmund, I don't like this unnatural treatment. When I asked their permission that I might take pity on him, they took from me the use of my own house — charged me, on pain of perpetual displeasure, neither to speak of him, plead for him, nor in any way sustain him.
EDMUND. Most savage and unnatural!

GLOUCESTER. Listen — say nothing. There is division between the Dukes, and a worse matter than that. I have received a letter this night — it's dangerous to speak of — I have locked the letter in my closet. These injuries the King now bears will be fully avenged.
